To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the probability of examination is not the sole determinant of the probability of a click, but that (ii) the probability of relevance is the primary determinant of the probability that a result will be clicked, given that it is examined.

(1) the CTR of sponsored results varies with the click pattern in prior positions due to both relevance and user behavior; (2) a user browsing model that attributes CCR change solely to relevance does better than a user browsing model which attributes the change solely to user behavior; and (3) it is essential to measure the quality of user browsing models in terms of accuracy in predicting relevance and not solely CCR.

(a) the probability of examination is a poor predictor of CTR; (b) the probability of relevance is a good predictor of CTR, but not as good as a model that combines examination with relevance; (c) the probability of relevancy is a good predictor in its own right, not just a predictor of CTR.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: 1) The impact of prior clicks on the relevance and examination of a given result, 2) The accuracy of user browsing models in predicting relevance and CTR, and 3) The impact of different user browsing models on search engine optimization.
user browsing behavior in sponsored search and how this behavior affects the design of sponsored search systems.
the following questions: How does a user’s examination of search results depend on the relevance of the prior results?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the best user browsing model depends on the goal: if the goal is predicting CTR, the model that considers both relevance and examination is best; but if the goal is to predict relevance, the model attributing all CTR change to changes in relevance does better.
a model that attributes all CTR change to changes in relevance does as well as a more complex model in predicting relevance and does substantially better than a simpler model in predicting CTR.
the user browsing models that assume relevance changes are important in explaining CTR changes do better in predicting CTR than those that assume that examination changes are important.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best user browsing models for sponsored search are those that attribute CTR change to changes in relevance.
, for sponsored searches, a substantial portion (about 30%) of the change in the CTR of an item when conditioned on the pattern of prior clicks is due to changes in relevance.
relevance is the dominant factor in user browsing models, and should be the primary focus for modeling user behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to distinguish between the probability of relevance and the probability of examination, and that the former may be more important than the latter in predicting CTR.
user browsing models that do not attribute CTR changes to relevance, but only to examination, are not as good as those that do.
user browsing models that attribute changes in CTR to changes in relevance can yield better predictions of CTR and relevance than models that attribute the changes to examination.
